c.tagline: The walled 'City of Popes,' with a monumental Gothic palace and the legendary broken Pont Saint-Bénézet

card: Widely accepted; cash useful for small market stalls

taxi.fare: Metered, roughly €3.50 flag fall plus per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard and reliable

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that connects to police, fire, and ambulance

walk: The walled old town is compact and entirely walkable; a car or bus is useful for day trips into Provence

safety.safety: Very safe city, popular with visitors of all ages
safety.crime: Petty theft near the Palais des Papes and train station is the main concern

hood_landmark.Intra-Muros (Walled Old Town): The Palais des Papes and Place de l'Horloge
hood_landmark.Île de la Barthelasse: The Île de la Barthelasse riverside park island
hood_landmark.Villeneuve-lès-Avignon: Fort Saint-André and the Tour Philippe-le-Bel above the Rhône

avoid.reason: The Monclar and Rocade housing estates south of the train station are best avoided at night.
Pickpockets target festival crowds in July and the area around the train station after dark.

hood_desc: The entire historic city within its medieval ramparts, home to the Palais des Papes and most restaurants and hotels; the natural base for any visit.
A rural river island just across the Rhône, offering cycling paths, farms, and a quiet green escape from the walled city.

The old cardinals' town on the Gard bank of the Rhône, a short walk or bus ride over the bridge from Avignon and technically in another département. Fort Saint-André, the Tour Philippe-le-Bel and the Chartreuse du Val de Bénédiction stand over quiet lanes, and rooms run cheaper and calmer than inside the walls.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, as throughout France.

transit.sys: Orizo (formerly TCRA) urban bus and tram network
transit.pay: Cash or contactless card on board; rechargeable travel card available
transit.note: The walled old town is pedestrian-friendly; buses mainly serve outlying neighborhoods and the TGV station

transport.air: Avignon-Provence Airport (AVN) has limited flights; Marseille Provence (MRS) is a larger option about 1 hr away
transport.train: TGV high-speed rail connects Avignon to Paris (under 3 hr) and Marseille
transport.bus: Regional buses connect to Luberon villages and other Provence towns
transport.car: Well connected via the A7 motorway; the old town is best explored on foot

airport.name: Marseille Provence Airport (main regional gateway)
airport.transport: Train via Marseille Saint-Charles, or rental car

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ap: An Orange, SFR, or Bouygues tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up is appreciated for guides and tours
tip.r: Service is included by law; rounding up is a nice gesture, not expected

landmarks: Palais des Papes (Palace of the Popes)
Europe's largest Gothic palace, this UNESCO-listed fortress housed nine popes in the 14th century and dominates Avignon with battlemented grandeur.
Pont Saint-Bénézet (Pont d'Avignon)
The legendary half-ruined medieval bridge of the famous French song, its four surviving arches reaching photogenically into the Rhône.
Cathédrale Notre-Dame des Doms
A Romanesque cathedral beside the papal palace, crowned by a gleaming gilded statue of the Virgin visible across the city.
Rocher des Doms
A panoramic clifftop garden above the Rhône with duck ponds and shaded paths, delivering postcard views of the bridge and Mont Ventoux.
Remparts d'Avignon (City Walls)
Over four kilometers of remarkably intact 14th-century ramparts still encircle the old town, punctuated by crenellated towers and grand gates.
Place de l'Horloge
The lively café-lined main square beneath the Gothic clock tower, home to the ornate town hall and opera house.
Musée du Petit Palais
A former cardinal's palace displaying a superb collection of medieval and Renaissance masterpieces, including a luminous Botticelli Madonna.
Rue des Teinturiers
A cobbled, plane-tree-shaded lane along a canal with still-turning waterwheels, once the heart of Avignon's textile-dyeing trade.
Les Halles d'Avignon
The covered market behind a living green wall, where Provençal producers pile stalls with olives, cheese, truffles, and tapenade.
Fort Saint-André (Villeneuve-lès-Avignon)
Across the Rhône, this mighty 14th-century royal fortress and its abbey gardens gaze back at Avignon's papal skyline.

train.note: Avignon has two stations: Avignon Centre just outside the city walls for TER and some TGV services, and Avignon TGV about 4 km south, linked to the centre by a frequent free shuttle train that takes 5 minutes. The one direct international service is the daily Barcelona train from Avignon TGV, which takes just under 4 hours and is sold by Renfe rather than SNCF - book it on renfe.com, where the fare is usually cheaper than on resellers. Everything else towards Italy, Switzerland or northern Europe means changing at Lyon Part-Dieu or Marseille Saint-Charles. Check carefully which station your ticket uses, as the two are not walkable from one another.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the gare routiere immediately beside Avignon Centre station, just outside Porte de la Republique. Tickets for FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus are booked online; the counter here mainly handles regional Zou! services (https://zou.maregionsud.fr/) to Nimes, Arles, Carpentras and the Luberon villages. Barcelona is roughly 6-7 hours by coach against under 4 by the direct train, so buses are the budget rather than the fast option. Passport or ID card is needed for the Spanish and Italian runs.

ferry.note: Avignon stands on the Rhone about 80 km from the Mediterranean, so there are no sea ferries. A free municipal river shuttle crosses to the Ile de la Barthelasse from below the Rocher des Doms in season, and river cruise ships tie up on the Rhone quays, but neither is a scheduled passenger ferry. The nearest ports with international sailings are Sete and Marseille, both about an hour away by train.

half.name: Pont du Gard
half.blurb: A three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge spanning the Gardon River, one of the best-preserved ancient Roman structures in the world.

half.name: Les Baux-de-Provence
half.blurb: A hilltop village built into limestone cliffs in the Alpilles mountains, with a ruined medieval castle and sweeping views over Provence.

half.name: Arles
half.blurb: A Roman city on the Rhône with a well-preserved amphitheater and ancient theater, where Van Gogh painted many of his best-known works.

half.name: Orange
half.blurb: A Provençal town home to one of the most intact Roman theaters in Europe, still used for opera performances each summer.

half.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
half.blurb: A wine village built around a ruined 14th-century papal castle, known for producing some of the Rhône Valley's most prized reds.
